name: White noise machine
lead: A white noise machine is a device that plays a steady, broadband sound intended to calm the listener or mask other noise. Despite the name, many such devices produce pink noise, whose power falls off at higher frequencies, or other noise colours or nature-like sounds, because true white noise sounds harsh [1]. They are used as sleep aids, for power-napping, for sound masking and privacy, and by some people with tinnitus [1].

In sleep-focused looksmaxxing, a machine is used to reduce wake-ups from traffic, neighbours or household noise, on the premise that better sleep supports appearance and recovery. Published evidence is mixed in scope: trials in hospital patients have reported improved sleep measures, while a 2024 scoping review raised concerns about continuous noise exposure in early childhood [3][4].

Volume is the main safety issue discussed in the literature. A paper cited by Wikipedia found that all 14 machines tested at maximum volume exceeded the 50 dB level considered safe for infants, and three exceeded the 85 dB adult threshold [1].

paras: Simple mechanical machines consist of an enclosed fan, sometimes with a speed switch, that pushes air through slots in the casing to make the sound; most modern units are electronic and play real-time generated or recorded audio [1]. Digital models often add Bluetooth, timers, volume limits and apps, and offer sounds such as rain, wind, ocean waves or traffic, sometimes blended with noise [1][2]. Electric fans are a common alternative; Wikipedia notes that some Asian communities historically avoided fans overnight because of a superstition about suffocation [1].

The Marpac Dohm, invented in 1962, is frequently credited as the original domestic fan-based white noise machine [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, attributes the first prototype to Rubbermaid executive James Buckwalter, who is said to have been inspired by a noisy motel stay, and to a 1964 patent for a sleep-inducing sound device filed with William Lahey and sold under Marpac brands [2]; that account has not been independently verified here. A 2017 Lancet Neurology historical note describes a seventeenth-century white noise machine associated with the sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini [5].

The usual explanation is masking: a constant sound reduces the contrast between background and sudden noises, so sleepers are less likely to be roused by them [2]. Manufacturers of sound-masking devices recommend a comfortable starting volume, and manufacturers of sleep aids recommend a level slightly above normal music listening level but within a comfortable range [1].

A 2021 systematic review in Sleep Medicine Reviews examined noise as a sleep aid [6], and a 2022 systematic review in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine examined auditory stimulation and sleep [7]. Abstracts were not available to this article, so their detailed findings are not summarised here.

A randomized trial published in 2026 in a Taiwanese medical centre assigned 58 intensive care patients to white noise at 40 to 50 dB from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. for three nights or to routine care; the white noise group had greater reductions in total sleep scores and sleep disturbance and better sleep effectiveness on later days according to the Verran and Snyder-Halpern scale [3].

In a 2016 randomized trial of 120 hospitalised adults, all participants received an eye mask, earplugs and a white noise machine, and some also received education on their use. The educated group had a larger fall in fatigue scores, with trends toward improvement in other measures that were not statistically significant [8]. Because the tools were given together, the trial does not isolate the white noise machine.

A 2024 scoping review of 20 studies (seven animal, 13 paediatric, including 9,428 human subjects) on continuous white noise exposure during sleep and childhood development noted that machines can exceed 91 dB at maximum volume, reported deleterious effects of continuous moderate-intensity noise in animal models, and said human data generally agreed while also suggesting that low-intensity noise may be beneficial during sleep [4]. A cross-sectional 2026 survey of 253 parents at a paediatric otolaryngology clinic found 59.3 percent used white noise, mostly from a bedroom machine played overnight, mainly to improve sleep and to mask environmental noise [9].

The main concern is sound level, especially for infants. Wikipedia reports that machines tested at maximum volume exceeded recommended levels for babies, and some also exceeded adult occupational limits [1]. The scoping review's authors warned that white noise machines used incorrectly may be associated with poorer hearing, speech and learning outcomes in children [4]. Some adults find constant sound disruptive.

Machines appear in sleep-environment routines alongside blackout curtains, masks and cooler rooms. Claims about appearance benefits rely on the indirect link between sleep and skin or recovery; the sources reviewed contain no studies of white noise machines and appearance outcomes.

Features commonly cited include a choice of sound types, a volume limiter, timers, battery or USB operation for travel, and non-looping audio. Prices usually range from about $20 to $50, with higher-end models around $100 [2]. Because of the volume findings above, maximum output level is a specification discussed in the research literature [1][4].

timeline.event: The Marpac Dohm, a fan-based machine, is introduced and often credited as the first domestic white noise machine [1].
A patent for a sleep-inducing sound device is reported to have been granted to Buckwalter and Lahey, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia [2].
